summary: Builds the language of statistical analysis (mean, median, mode, range, outlier, correlation, plus data/sample/frequency and chart words) for 9–11 year-olds by attaching each term to what it tells us about real data, not to a recited definition or a single add-and-divide rule. The core teaching move is contrasting the three measures of centre on the SAME data set — especially a skewed one — so 'mean', 'median' and 'mode' come apart instead of collapsing into 'the average', naming range as ONE number (a distance), tying 'outlier' to its pull on the mean, and keeping 'correlation' as direction-of-trend distinct from causation. Activities span a draggable live data set (primary builder of meaning), use-in-context narration, categorisation/matching checks, an in-role data detective, and a static glossary reference — each with a different pedagogical purpose.
misconceptions: Treating 'average'/mean as only the add-and-divide rule, with no sense of what the number represents about the data
Swapping the measures of centre: calling the most frequent value the 'average', or finding the median without ordering / from the frequency column
Giving 'range' as the two extreme values ('0 and 8') rather than their difference (8)
Using 'correlation' for any relationship and sliding it into causation ('taller people cause bigger feet'), or calling a patternless scatter 'correlated'
Not connecting an outlier to its effect — assuming the mean sits in the middle regardless of an extreme value

activities.title: Draggable data set: watch the measures behave differently
steps: Start with a small, meaningful data set shown as dots on a value strip — e.g. goals a team scored across seven matches: 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 2, 8 (ordered: 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 8, so the mode is a single clear value, 2).
Read the mean, median, mode and range displayed and labelled live beside the data, each with a one-line 'what it tells us'.
Drag one match's score (say the 3) up to 20 and watch the mean slide up to chase it, the median barely move, and the mode stay unchanged — the moment the three labelled numbers behave DIFFERENTLY.
Drag a value far from the rest to create an outlier, then recompute the mean with and without it and compare how little the median shifts.
See the range marked on a number line as the labelled distance from lowest to highest, so it reads as one number, not two.

Switch to a scatter panel (e.g. height vs shoe size) and move a correlation slider from negative through none to positive, labelled as the trend's direction, with a standing caption 'a link, not a cause'.
activities.insight: Mean, median and mode are not interchangeable words for 'average': they track different things, and seeing them respond differently to the same change is what pulls the words apart. The mean is influenced by every value, so an outlier drags it while the median hardly moves; range is a single distance; correlation names the direction of a trend, not a cause.

activities.title: Narrate the data: use the words for the right thing
steps: Take a small real data set — e.g. 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 2, 8 — and a scatter graph of height against shoe size, and tell the story of the data aloud using mean, median, mode and range as you go.

For each term, say not just the value but what it tells us: the mode is the most frequent value (2, appearing three times); the median is the middle AFTER ordering (2); the mean (≈2.57) is a typical / fair-share score; the range is 8, the difference 8−0.
Name the 8 as an outlier and say what it does — it drags the mean UP while the median barely moves.
Describe the scatter with the right word: 'positive correlation' meaning taller children tend to have bigger feet — a link, not a cause.

Answer follow-up probes: 'What does that 2.57 actually tell us about how this team scores?'; 'Why did you have to order the numbers for the median but not the mode?'; 'If that 8 had been 80, which number would change most and which hardly at all?'; 'Does being tall MAKE feet grow, or is there a word for the link without saying one causes the other?'
activities.insight: Owning the vocabulary means using each word for the thing it names when describing freely — not reciting definitions. Narrating real data exposes and corrects swaps (mode called 'average', range given as two numbers, correlation slid into cause) that a definition task would let a child recite around.

activities.title: Match and sort: check correct use, not definitions
steps: On a given ordered data set, match each word — mean, median, mode, range — to the value it names.
Sort a set of scatter graphs into positive / negative / no correlation.
Choose which sentence uses 'range' correctly, where a distractor names the two extreme values ('0 and 8') instead of their difference (8).
Judge statements as 'uses the word correctly' or 'incorrectly' (e.g. 'the median is the middle of the unordered list', 'the mode is the average').
activities.insight: Correct use can be probed by matching and categorising against a data context — this surfaces swaps without asking the child to recite a definition.

activities.title: Data detective: catch the swap in conversation
steps: Take on a 'data detective' role: a character presents a data story and asks the child to describe it.
Describe the data aloud, choosing the right statistical words.
Respond when the character echoes back correct usage or queries a misuse — e.g. 'You said the range is 0 and 8 — can a range be two numbers?'
activities.insight: Talking through a data story and being gently pressed on word choice surfaces swaps in the moment and rehearses precise use.

activities.title: Glossary reference: anchor each term to its meaning
steps: On a fixed, annotated data set, reveal cards for 'mean', 'median', 'mode', 'range' and 'outlier', each giving what it names and a one-line 'what it tells us' with an example.
Use the glossary as a reference while working on the other activities.
activities.insight: Each term is tied to a one-line meaning and an example, giving a stable reference point for the vocabulary.

checkQuestion: Give the child a small real data set — e.g. goals a team scored in seven matches: 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 8 — and a simple scatter graph of, say, height against shoe size for the class. Set a talking task, NOT a definition task: 'Tell me the story of this team's scoring — use the words mean, median, mode and range as you go, and say what each one tells us. There's an 8 in there: what would you call that value, and what does it do to the mean? Now look at this scatter graph and describe the relationship using the right word.' Listen for which terms they USE and whether each is used for the right thing. (Do not ask 'what does mean/range/correlation mean?' — listen for correct USE in the description.)
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE: mode = 2 (most frequent), median = 2 (the middle AFTER ordering), mean ≈ 2.4 and a sense of what it represents (a fair-share / typical score), range = 7 (the difference 8−0, one number), the 8 named as an outlier that pulls the mean UP (because the mean is influenced by every value) while the median barely moves, and the scatter described with 'positive correlation' meaning taller children tend to have bigger feet — a link, not stated as a cause. Terms used precisely and for the right thing is mastery.
